My argument is that Proportional Representation misses the point, as what we should really be attempting to achieve is proportional influence, which is not necessarily the same thing as representation.

To take a hypothetical, let's say our parliament utilises PR, and currently Party A has 52% of seats, Party B 38% and Party C 10%. Now an election is held and the results for the new parliament are Party A 48%, B 47% and C 5%.

In this new parliament C has seen their support half, yet they're clearly in a more influential position, so long as you need 50% +1 to pass any bill.

The thing about a Parliament is it's all built around getting a majority. A bill which has 51% of the House vote "Yes/aye" and 49% vote "No/Nay" passes just as much as a bill which has 100% of the support.

For this reason parliaments will naturally have a tendency to move into two blocks, because the parties are all trying to get 50% + 1 of the total House to support their bill. Even in PR systems, you find there is generally a large centre-right party, who is supported by smaller right wing or centrists when in government, and a large centre-left party, who is supported by smaller left wing or centrists when its in government. Both the main right party and the main left party are still trying to get that 50% + 1 support.

This does not mean I support a system where smaller voices are not heard. In the Australian preference system, one can vote for a smaller party to give them some support, whilst still second or third preferencing a larger party so as to not throw away their vote.

The advantage of this is that Australia is nearly always government by a majority (One hung parliament has occurred since the end of WWII), but at the same time smaller parties have influence on the debate, as larger parties are forced to make concessions to the supporters of minor parties in order to receive their preferences.

For example, in Australia the dominant centre left Labor Party cannot completely disregard the left of centre Greens party, because they need preferences from the Greens in order to win elections. The Greens may not have proportional representation in the Parliament, but they have proportional influence, because they cannot be ignored by major parties.

The exception to this is Parliaments where you need a super majority to pass certain motions, in which case obviously 50% + 1 is less powerful than 100%. However, the majority of legislation passed in the majority of parliaments or congresses around the world requires the simple majority.
Alternative Voting (like in the Australian House of Representatives) is a superior voting system to Proportional Representation

The argument is going to continue to be: Free speech is only protected legally, private companies get to host or not host whatever they want and that's their choice. It's like trying to fight a private school over its curriculum, as long as students are enrolling and paying, they can keep teaching whatever they want. In your comparison, it's like trying to tell a private citizen he can't burn books on his property - as long as the government isn't responsible for it, there's no legal recourse.

The problem comes as more and more corporations own larger and larger pieces of the internet, and ultimately, our collective voice. Think about it, without internet access how would you spread information to others that you think's important? You'd have to start a local newsletter or buy slots on cable access, and even then you're only reaching people immediately local to you. Corporate media knows the internet is our easiest, cheapest method of information diffusion, if they can stifle the internet they know we don't have the capital to go out and start our own media companies.

Yes, it's the commercialisation of the internet (and more and more physical space) that will be the death of diversity of expression. I hate to keep harping on about Reddit but when I first arrived there about 6 years ago my first thought was "this is how the internet used to be". Crappy graphics but loads of great content powered but the passion of enthusiasts. More and more the internet has been commercialised, and that means homogenised. The Guardian newspaper runs a viral video chart most weeks. It used to be all sorts of weirdness. Now it's mostly viral marketing and pop videos .

On your second point, there's nothing stopping someone from creating their own webpage and sharing whatever content they like (pretty much the role Voat is playing at present). It doesn't mean that the broader community will see what you say, but there can't really be any expectation of that (a person can stand on a soap box on the corner and shout about the end of the world, but it's everyone's right to keep listening to their mp3s as they pass by). If the broader public continue to use commercialized services that serve up sanitized content, then it's their own damn fault if they miss something important. Trying to motivate them to listen is probably as hard as motivating some people to be interested in politics.

What bothers me is people use the fact that our Constitution only protects our speech from the government as an excuse to not support free speech when it's under attack from these corporations.

Legally, they're right. And I don't necessarily want to fight them in a legal sense. I still don't want to support them and will have something to say about it.

I'm going to assume that by "Burning Books" you mean it in the sense of what Hitler did, or what is done in Farhenheit 451. That is, an effort is made to burn every copy of some particular book, and make sure that new copies don't surface.

Given the vast size of the internet, doing the same with threads/comments as books (in regard to what I wrote before), is impossible. Hell, it is even impossible to burn every book and outlaw every copy of a book today. I'm obvisouly focusing on books/threads/comments pertaining to something that isn't considered a crime everywhere, e.g., how-to books on molesting children (which probably still exists and is obtainable, just not easily). If you somehow where able to remove every single comment/thread pertaining to some specific topic, from the internet, then I guess you could compare the two. I personally believe this to be utterly impossible, especially when it comes to legal but controversial opinions (see for example how FPH got an outlet on fph.io and here after reddit threw them out).

If you then talk about book burning in the more casual non-dystopian sense then consider this: If I have a book that I can't sell, don't wan't and otherwise can't get rid off, am I then wrong for burning that book? If I have a website where people can make threads and comment on these threads, am I then wrong for removing unwanted content? For example: Does advertising for shady looking porn sites belong in the comment section of a news outlet? No, probably not.

edit: added an example.

Not necessarily. For example, I deleted a couple links in the music subs I mod the other day because they fell outside the subverse's specified rules. Each time I messaged the poster and informed them why their thread was being deleted and which rule was being broken. I wouldn't consider that equivalent to book burning because the rule was plainly stated in the sidebar. Subs have to have some kind of rules and guidelines for content or it is pointless to even create them.

There is a big difference between good faith rule enforcement and capricious censorship.
